newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian army prefers to end civil war peacefully.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian army prefers to end civil war peacefully.

text.p: Cambodian troops could take the last stronghold of Khmer Rouge guerrillas within one month, but would prefer to end the country's long-running civil war peacefully, senior military officials said on Tuesday.

The boast came amid a build-up of forces in recent days around the rebels' northern base of Anlong Veng as negotiations for the defection of the guerrillas and the release of 15 government officials in their hands appeared to stall.

"If we want to fight...We will take only one month to capture Anlong Veng before Khmer New Year (April 13-15) because we have more troops and ammunition. We have helicopters, we have artillery and we ask the Thai government to shut the border," said an army general by telephone from the northwest province of Siem Reap.
But the general, who asked not to be named, added, "We do not want to do this as we are tired of more than two decades of war, but we cannot let Ta Mok do what he wants."

He was referring to the feared one-legged Khmer Rouge military chief Ta Mok. He has been holding 15 officials and pilots who flew into Khmer Rouge by helicopter in mid-February to try and persuade the rebels to defect as thousands of others have done.
Government officials, including co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh, warned last week that Ta Mok should hand back the 15 soon or face attack.

Long Sereirath, deputy commander of military region covering Anlong Veng, said on Tuesday, "Ta Mok has asked the government to agree with his many conditions quickly before he and Anlong Veng join...but some conditions the government cannot accept."
He would not elaborate on the conditions, but another official involved in negotiations said the Khmer Rouge in Anlong Veng wanted guarantees that their leaders would be save from retribution.
Ta Mok and others are implicated in the deaths of more than one million people during the brutal 1975-79 Khmer Rouge rule.
Armed forces deputy chief of staff Meas Sophea, meanwhile, downplayed the build-up of forces, saying they included troop rotations and were aimed at protecting posts from rebel attacks.
"During the week the government has sent some troops to the north to replace soldiers there but we have no intention to fight Anlong Veng," he said, confirming that weapons had also been sent.
He acknowledged there had been clashes between government troops and Khmer Rouge guerrillas in the northern province of Preah Vihear.
The Khmer Rouge have been severely weakened by thousands of defections in the past six months and are believed to numebr fewer than 2,000, mostly in and around Anlong Veng.
The Maoist-inspired guerrillas signed a U.N.-sponsored peace in 1991, but reneged on the deal and have been fightng the coalition government which came to power after 1993 elections.
